{"id": "26:166/q09", "question": "What does ʿādūn mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:166/q09/p1", "position": "Transgressors who go beyond lawful or just limits.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn Jurayj give the basic gloss. Yaḥyā says beyond God's command; al-Ṭabarī and al-Baghawī specify crossing from permitted to prohibited sexual relations. Al-Wāḥidī says from lawful to unlawful and obedience to sin, and in al-Wajīz calls it utmost injustice. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, al-Elmalılı, and al-Iṣlāḥī describe exceeding limits, injustice, or proper human conduct. Jishumī equates ʿādī with muʿtadī and notes possible derivation from enmity or swift running."}]}
{"id": "26:166/q10", "question": "How broad is the charge of transgression?", "turns_on": "Whether the charge is confined to the grave sexual offense, extends to all sin, describes abnormal desire, or stresses an entrenched disposition or emotive rebuke.", "positions": [{"id": "26:166/q10/p1", "position": "It condemns their sexual offense as a grave crossing of bounds.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says they cross from God-permitted sexual relations to prohibited ones. Al-Rāzī and al-Bayḍāwī allow that the enormity alone makes them especially deserving of the label; al-Nasafī likewise singles out the grave act. Al-Biqāʿī says Lot rejects their evasion because they turned from wives to males; al-Ālūsī says they pursued what was not created for sex and left what was."}, {"id": "26:166/q10/p2", "position": "They transgress in all sins, with this act included.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī offers this as one alternative. Bursevī says the bounds are exceeded in all sins, and al-Ālūsī says the omitted complement of 'transgress' may be general."}, {"id": "26:166/q10/p3", "position": "They exceed the bounds of desire beyond other people and even animals.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī gives this as an alternative sense, while al-Ālūsī reports a version saying beyond people and most animals and allows a specific complement of excess in sexual desire."}, {"id": "26:166/q10/p4", "position": "Transgression is a settled trait that keeps them beyond God's bounds.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī calls it an entrenched disposition and says Lot's rebuke exposes that rooted condition."}, {"id": "26:166/q10/p5", "position": "The wording conveys sorrow over conduct beyond human nature.", "reasons": "Al-Iṣlāḥī reads the address as expressing yearning and sorrow at their crossing the limits of human nature."}]}
{"id": "26:166/q11", "question": "What does placing antum first add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:166/q11/p1", "position": "The direct pronoun singles them out and emphasizes their notorious transgression.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says the address makes them alone conspicuous for exceeding limits; al-Ālūsī transmits Abū Ḥayyān's explanation."}]}
{"id": "26:166/q12", "question": "What ruling on anal intercourse with wives or enslaved women is drawn from this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse's restriction to the lawful part of spouses establishes prohibition; the notes also point to 2:223 and a hadith.", "positions": [{"id": "26:166/q12/p1", "position": "It is forbidden, and intercourse with wives that way is a major sin.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī says the verse forbids it with wives and female slaves and strongly faults those permitting it. {"id": "26:166/q13", "question": "What penalty is assigned for male same-sex intercourse?", "turns_on": "The jurists differ over whether the act receives discretionary punishment, stoning in all cases, or the fornication rule.", "positions": [{"id": "26:166/q13/p1", "position": "Discretionary taʿzīr applies, without a fixed ḥadd.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports Abū Ḥanīfa's ruling and says his two disciples disagree."}, {"id": "26:166/q13/p2", "position": "Both participants are stoned, married or unmarried.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports Mālik's ruling."}, {"id": "26:166/q13/p3", "position": "The penalty follows the legal rule for fornication.", "reasons": "Bursevī attributes this to al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad."}]}
{"id": "26:166/q14", "question": "What does this rebuke imply about human freedom and divine creation of acts?", "turns_on": "Whether moral blame and 'leaving' require self-originated acts, or whether divine knowledge and the origin of motives make that inference fail.", "positions": [{"id": "26:166/q14/p1", "position": "People must originate their acts for blame, praise, commands, and prohibitions to be coherent.", "reasons": "Al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār argues that 'leaving' presumes an ability to act otherwise, whereas what God creates would be imposed; blaming divinely created transgression would resemble blaming skin color. Al-Rāzī summarizes that case and notes this story's special force beyond the commands and blame in the stories of Moses, Abraham, and Noah."}, {"id": "26:166/q14/p2", "position": "Divine knowledge and the cause of a decisive motive defeat that free-will argument.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī answers that nonoccurrence of acts God knows will occur is impossible without making divine knowledge ignorance, so a command to avoid them would demand the impossible. A choice needs a preponderant motive: if a person originates that motive its causes regress infinitely; if God originates it, compulsion follows. He says these two arguments defeat al-Qāḍī's case."}]}

{"id": "26:167/q04", "question": "How should mīm be pronounced in this verse and comparable environments?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:167/q04/p1", "position": "Mīm remains nasal; a vocalized mīm avoids emphatic coloring, while a sākin mīm is clear before most letters and assimilates with ghunna before another mīm.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says the ghunna of assimilated or sākin mīm comes from the nose; he warns against coloring vocalized mīm, especially before emphatic letters or alif. {"id": "26:167/q08", "question": "What do they threaten will happen to Lot?", "turns_on": "Whether 'expelled' means removal alive, possibly in humiliating conditions, or removal of his corpse after killing him.", "positions": [{"id": "26:167/q08/p1", "position": "They will expel him from their town and community.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and others locate the expulsion in their town, land, or midst. {"id": "26:167/q14", "question": "What sīn-to-ṣād sound shift is described in the associated linguistic notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:167/q14/p1", "position": "Some speakers change sīn to ṣād near a retracted or emphatic consonant, especially qāf, without extending the change to less similar consonants.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives صقت and صبقت with qāf and explains that ṣād matches its raised articulation; صالغ and صلخ show the effect of ġayn and ḫāʾ. {"id": "26:216/q05", "question": "What does the Prophet's declaration of being innocent of what they do entail?", "turns_on": "Whether the object of disavowal is conduct alone, people together with conduct, the broader withdrawal of support expressed by barāʾa, or in the inward reading human power itself.", "positions": [{"id": "26:216/q05/p1", "position": "He repudiates their wrong deeds, especially unbelief and idol worship, without bearing responsibility for them or necessarily repudiating the people.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn al-Jawzī name shirk, idol worship, unbelief or disobedience as the acts repudiated. Yaḥyā ibn Sallām, al-Naḥḥās, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī describe rejection of conduct. Al-Ḥusayn, reported by al-Sulamī, says Muhammad unlike other prophets rejects deeds rather than kin themselves because of his rank and intercession, which lifts the darkness of sins; Abū Ḥayyān likewise preserves intercession for sinful believers. Iṣlāḥī includes his efforts to share night prayer's blessings with companions."}, {"id": "26:218/q04/p9", "position": "He rises to call, warn, or act for the religious mission.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī transmits rising to summon people to Islam; al-Ṭabrisī gives rising to warn and deliver the message. {"id": "26:218/q06", "question": "How did the Prophet maintain night prayer?", "turns_on": "The reports describe distinct circumstances: praying seated when able to continue and making up a missed vigil.", "positions": [{"id": "26:218/q06/p1", "position": "He never omitted it, praying seated when ill or tired.", "reasons": "Bursawī transmits ʿĀʾisha's report of the Prophet's persistent night prayer and seated prayer during illness or fatigue."}, {"id": "26:218/q06/p2", "position": "If he missed it through illness or another cause, he made up twelve cycles during the day.", "reasons": "Bursawī attributes the report to Muslim."}]}
{"id": "26:218/q07", "question": "What is the special merit of night prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:218/q07/p1", "position": "It is the best prayer after the obligatory prayer and merits making up when missed.", "reasons": "Bursawī quotes a prophetic report calling it the best prayer after obligatory prayer; he says tahajjud exceeds other voluntary prayers in merit, so it is made up although ordinary supererogatory prayers are not."}]}
{"id": "26:218/q08", "question": "How does the verse fit its surrounding discourse?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the wording to the preceding reliance and mercy, the adjoining mention of prostrators, the sūrah's opening, or a parallel account of prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "26:218/q08/p1", "position": "The description after the command to rely on God grounds reliance in His care and support.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī connects awareness of the Prophet's state to promised victory and help for allies, reassuring him; al-Biqāʿī grounds divine sufficiency in encompassing knowledge that secures benefit and averts harm; Bursawī says seeing explains the promised mercy. {"id": "26:218/q09", "question": "What inward rising and divine vision are described?", "turns_on": "Whether the inward reading traces stages of resurrection or calls for sustained awareness of divine watchfulness.", "positions": [{"id": "26:218/q09/p1", "position": "God accompanies and preserves the Prophet through successive spiritual resurrections.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī names the minor resurrection, the intermediate primordial state, and the major resurrection in unity and steadfastness."}, {"id": "26:218/q09/p2", "position": "Awareness of divine watchfulness calls for steadiness in absence and presence.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī says one never escapes the watch of divine power; the Najmī interpretations quoted by Bursawī say God's sight of intention draws attention from creatures to hidden states."}]}
